title: Maryam, whole
hook: Zakariyya, Maryam, Ibrahim, Musa, Isma'il, Idris (Surah 19)
tomorrow: why would God tell Musa to take off his shoes?

segments.voice: Yesterday, hidden mercy: a holed boat, a rebuilt wall, and reasons that came late. Today the mercy is out in the open, from the very first line.

Every group project has the question that starts the argument: who counts as a lead? The Qur'an has a surah named for a woman, Maryam, the mother of Isa, and it carries a question classical scholars argued over in plain sight. Was she a prophet? The surah opens, in Pickthall's words: "A mention of the mercy of thy Lord unto His servant Zachariah." And then it keeps going, person after person, mercy after mercy, until the end.
screen: `WHO COUNTS AS A LEAD?` → `A SURAH NAMED FOR A WOMAN.` → `WAS SHE A PROPHET?`

segments.voice: Read it whole and the shape is a procession. Zakariyya, old, crying to his Lord in secret for a child, and given Yahya. Maryam, alone, visited by the angel, giving birth beneath a palm, and the baby who speaks from the cradle. Then Ibrahim pleading gently with his father, Musa called near, Isma'il true to his promise, Idris raised high. Through all of it a name keeps coming back: ar-Rahman, the Beneficent. Now the debate. Maryam's section opens the way the prophets' sections do: "And make mention of Mary in the Scripture." One view, held by some classical scholars, Ibn Hazm among them: yes, she was a prophet. An angel spoke to her, and God's word came to her; what else is prophecy? The other view: prophethood was given to men, and the surah calls Ibrahim, Musa, Isma'il and Idris prophets in so many words, but not her. Another verse calls her siddiqa, a woman of truth. Both views honor her; the Qur'an says she was chosen above the women of the worlds. Neither side lowers her by an inch; the argument is over a title, not over her place. What the surah itself insists on is the thread: mercy, passed from one person to the next. A child given to an old man. A mother fed by a palm tree. A father answered with peace. Whatever the title, the mercy moves through each of them.
screen: `A PROCESSION OF THE MERCIFUL.` · `THE SAME OPENING AS THE PROPHETS.` · `YES: AN ANGEL SPOKE TO HER.` · `NO: A WOMAN OF TRUTH.` · then, large: `MERCY THROUGH THE PROPHETS.`

segments.voice: Read the surah's first line aloud, slowly: a mention of the mercy of thy Lord unto His servant Zachariah. Then, for the sit, bring to mind one person whose kindness reached you without any title attached, and let them stand in the procession for a while.
screen: `READ ONE LINE ALOUD.` · `ONE PERSON, NO TITLE.`

segments.voice: Maryam. The mother of Isa, and the name of a whole surah that walks through the prophets on a road paved with mercy.
The line to keep: mercy through the prophets, whatever title each one carries. Surah Maryam, read aloud.

howItsDone: Surah Maryam is recited in Arabic in prayer and at home; Muslims honor Maryam as the mother of Isa, and scholars have held different views on whether she should be called a prophet.

fork.reveal: that's the strongest form of the 'no' view: the surah's explicit titles, and siddiqa in 5:75. the 'yes' view answers that an angel spoke to her. both honor her.

chat.meaning: Classical scholars disagreed: some held Maryam was a prophet because an angel spoke to her; others called her siddiqa, a woman of truth. Both views honor her.

notes: Pickthall 19:2 and 19:16 match earlier days (92, 744); confirm.

Debate: Ibn Hazm (al-Fisal) and some others (e.g. al-Qurtubi, al-Ash'ari is sometimes cited) held that Maryam was a prophet because she received revelation through an angel; others held prophethood was for men and cite siddiqa (5:75). The voice names only Ibn Hazm and does not say which view was larger. Confirm the attribution and that both views are fairly stated.
'Calls Ibrahim, Musa, Isma'il and Idris prophets in so many words': 19:41, 19:51, 19:54, 19:56 each use nabi. Confirm.

Paraphrased: Zakariyya's secret cry (19:3), Yahya (19:7), the angel (19:17–19), the palm (19:23–25), the baby speaking (19:29–30), Ibrahim and his father, answered with peace (19:42–47), Musa called near (19:52), Isma'il true to his promise (19:54), Idris raised high (19:57), 3:42 chosen above the women of the worlds. Confirm.
'A name keeps coming back: ar-Rahman' describes the surah's repeated use of al-Rahman; no count is given. Confirm.
